The single biggest story of the week in Russia was the intense diplomatic push to end the war in Ukraine, layered with a dramatic escalation of military strikes on Russian soil. Here is a theme-by-theme reading of what actually happened between November 9 and 14, 2026.

PEACE TALKS AND THE US DIPLOMATIC PUSH. Russia and Ukraine held their second round of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11. The sessions were short, ending in under two hours on the second day, and produced one concrete result: the largest prisoner exchange of the war, as confirmed by Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, and Al Jazeera. Beyond that, the talks covered ceasefire monitoring, territory (including a US proposal that Ukraine cede parts of the Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, per Al Jazeera and TV5Monde), and a new European security framework. Russia's negotiator Medinsky reported "some progress" but no breakthrough. The US then sent envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow on November 12 to meet Putin directly. Putin was described as "uncompromising" by AFP and TV5Monde, and as "playing for time" by CNN. Witkoff told reporters progress was being made. The envoys then flew to Dublin to meet Zelensky, who called it a "window of opportunity." The headline takeaway: the US is driving the process, Russia is engaging but stalling, and Ukraine is cautiously optimistic. (Sources: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, FT, WSJ, CNBC, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

EUROPE'S ROLE IN THE TALKS. A sub-plot of the week was the fight over whether and how Europe participates. Putin initially said Europeans could join if they showed "readiness to contribute" (Reuters, Nov 13). Moscow then told Europe to pick a single envoy if it wants a seat at the table (FT). EU leaders squabbled over who to send (Bloomberg, DW, FT). Zelensky welcomed the prospect (Reuters, BBC). Europe fears a "Russian trap" (TV5Monde). Germany's Merz asked Trump for "no surprises" from the Putin talks (Reuters). This is still unresolved and will carry into next week.

THE TRUMP-XI-PUTIN TRILATERAL SUMMIT IN CHINA. Announced on November 13-14, this is the week's most consequential forward-looking event: Trump, Xi, and Putin will meet in Shenzhen on November 19, on the sidelines of APEC. It is the first three-way summit of the three great powers. The White House confirmed Trump will raise nuclear-arms cuts (Reuters, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ). The meeting evokes comparisons to Yalta in 1945 (AFP, Reuters). Beijing is described as facing a "Russia bind" (DW) and as wary of hosting (Reuters). The US balked at China's demand for a tightly scripted format (WSJ). This summit will dominate the second half of next week.

MILITARY ACTIONS ON RUSSIAN SOIL. The war is coming home to Russia in a very tangible way. Ukraine launched nearly 1,200 drones at Russia in a single day (AP, Nov 13). Ukraine hit its ninth Russian oil refinery since the start of November, including the biggest refinery in Siberia (Bloomberg). A drone attack sparked a fire at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, injuring three (Reuters, Bloomberg). A Ukrainian drone struck a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, detected by Finland (Reuters, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera). Two car bombs hit Moscow in two days: one killed a Russian soldier near St Petersburg in a targeted assassination (Reuters, Nov 12), the other badly injured a former aide to a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM (Reuters, BBC, CNN, DW, Al Jazeera). Ukraine claimed 3,000 Russian casualties in a single day (Al Jazeera). Russia's own records, per pirated official statistics, show over 400,000 Russian killed, and Al Jazeera reports the figure at 450,000. Over 11,000 foreign military deaths have been recorded by Russia (Bloomberg, TV5Monde). Russia also struck Ukrainian military factories, railways, food factories, and power infrastructure, with Kyiv facing winter blackouts (Reuters, DW, FT, BBC). (Sources: all outlets.)

RUSSIA'S ECONOMY, OIL, AND THE DIESEL DEAL. The Trump diesel deal, meant to bring Russian fuel back to US markets after sanctions were lifted, has stumbled. A tanker carrying Russian diesel made a U-turn off the US East Coast (WSJ, Bloomberg, Reuters). US companies are shunning the fuel (Reuters). Meanwhile, Russia's diesel exports to other markets doubled (FT), and oil revenues hit a five-month high (Bloomberg, CNBC). The IEA reported Russian fuel exports and oil output rebounded in October (Reuters). But the economy is slowing as Ukrainian strikes damage industry (Bloomberg). Russia is rationing petrol after refinery attacks (FT). Russia's push to replace the dollar with the Chinese yuan has collapsed (Bloomberg). Foreign businesses seized by Putin are helping fund the war machine (Bloomberg). (Sources: Bloomberg, FT, WSJ, CNBC, Reuters, Al Jazeera.)

SANCTIONS AND ECONOMIC PRESSURE. The EU agreed new sanctions listings on Russian banks, the shadow fleet, and misinformation operations (Reuters, Nov 11), with a formal package to be approved on Monday, November 17 (Reuters, Bloomberg). The UK sanctioned Russia's Slavneft oil producer (Reuters). Putin ordered a sanctioned Russian bank to seize a UK brokerage's assets (Bloomberg). The EU is also preparing Ukraine funding measures by year-end (Reuters). (Sources: Reuters, Bloomberg, FT.)

MEDIA, PRESS FREEDOM, AND INFORMATION WAR. Russia's last major independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, officially closed its Moscow newsroom after three decades, citing official pressure and eviction (Reuters, BBC, DW, CNN, TV5Monde). Two French deputies and two journalists from Le Monde and Ouest-France were barred from entering Russia (TV5Monde). Sberbank doubled down on AI after a drone attack on a data center (Reuters). Russia is using giant plastic bags to store unexported grain as Black Sea trade stalls (Reuters). (Sources: Reuters, BBC, DW, CNN, TV5Monde.)

ESPIONAGE AND INTELLIGENCE. A US Army soldier assigned to a NATO unit was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia (AP, BBC, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde). Russia arrested two suspected Polish spies in Kaliningrad (Reuters, Bloomberg). Romania's intelligence agency identified a Russian-linked cyber attack (Reuters). Norway's security service warned that Russian intelligence could carry out sabotage in the coming year (Reuters). The UK and Russia discussed the need for a new back channel to avoid miscalculation (FT). (Sources: all outlets.)

DOMESTIC POLITICS AND SOCIETY. A lawyer in Kaliningrad was sentenced to 12 years on treason charges (Reuters). Police raided Moscow gathering spots for young people (DW). Russia set cull limits to control the bear population after 36 bear attacks killed people (Reuters). Russia's ambassador to the US died suddenly at age 66 (Reuters, AP, CNN, Bloomberg). Russia's delegation visited Afghanistan to discuss trade with the Taliban (AP). Russia said military-to-military contacts with Britain are possible (Reuters). Russia said it could conclude non-aggression pacts with NATO members (Reuters). (Sources: Reuters, DW, AP, Bloomberg.)

SPORTS AND CULTURE. A wave of European countries barred Russian athletes: Norway (Reuters), Canada (Reuters, AP), Estonia (BBC), Finland (DW, Reuters). The IIHF filed a CAS challenge over Russia's reinstatement (Reuters). Russia threatened sanctions against Canada and Germany over the ice hockey dispute (DW). The NHL indicated Finland's block could affect future games (AP). (Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, DW.)

OTHER NOTABLE ITEMS. Russia's top independent newspaper closing was a symbolic blow to dissent. Zelensky warned of Moscow seeking to redraw "influence" in Europe (AFP). Russia's shadow war has entered a "dangerous new phase" (Bloomberg). The US warned Madagascar over growing military ties with Russia (BBC). A "beer-loving nations alliance" (UK, Netherlands, Baltic states) was launched against Russian naval activity (TV5Monde). Russia and Ukraine are racing to build military satellite networks (Al Jazeera).
measurement.expected:
THE TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT IN SHENZHEN (NOVEMBER 19). This is the anchor event of next week. Almost certain: the three leaders will sit down in Shenzhen on November 19. The White House, Kremlin, and Chinese state media have all confirmed it. Expect a joint photo op, a statement on nuclear arms reductions (Trump explicitly said he will raise this), and some language about Ukraine. The Yalta comparisons will dominate commentary. Xi is wary of being seen as the junior partner, so the format will be carefully managed. Putin will use the summit to signal to Europe that he has the US and China in his corner, potentially to buy time before the next round of Ukraine talks. I would not bet on any major breakthrough at the summit itself. It is more about positioning and optics than substance. Confidence: almost certain the meeting happens; probable that it produces a joint statement on nuclear arms; possible that it sets a framework for a follow-up Ukraine security discussion; unlikely that it resolves the Ukraine war.

EU SANCTIONS PACKAGE (NOVEMBER 17). Almost certain: the EU will formally adopt the new sanctions package on Monday, November 17, targeting Russian banks, the shadow fleet, and misinformation operations, as agreed by EU envoys on November 11 and confirmed by France (Reuters, Bloomberg). The UK will likely add its own measures around the same time. Russia will issue a strong but not dramatic response. The sanctions will hit Sberbank, VTB, and several shadow fleet vessels. Expect some minor market jitters in the ruble. Confidence: almost certain the package is adopted; probable that Russia announces countermeasures within 48 hours.

PRISONER EXCHANGE EXECUTION. Probable: the "largest prisoner exchange" agreed in Abu Dhabi will be physically carried out in the days after November 14. Kushner explicitly said the US is working toward it (Reuters). The logistics of moving hundreds of prisoners across a front line take time, so I expect the actual swap to happen between November 15 and 21, possibly timed to coincide with or follow the Shenzhen summit for maximum photo opportunity. Confidence: probable it happens this week; possible it slips to early next week.

EUROPEAN DELEGATION FOR PEACE TALKS. Probable: the EU will finalize who its envoy or delegation to the next round of Russia-Ukraine talks will be. Moscow has set the condition: pick one person (FT). The EU's internal squabbling (Bloomberg, DW, FT) will resolve by mid-week. Expect a mix of foreign ministers or national security aides (Bloomberg mentioned national security aides). The next round of talks, if it happens, would likely be in late November or early December. Confidence: probable the EU agrees on a representative; possible a new round of talks is scheduled before the end of the month.

CONTINUED DRONE STRIKES ON RUSSIAN INFRASTRUCTURE. Almost certain: Ukraine will continue hitting Russian refineries, ports, and industrial zones. Nine refineries have been hit in November alone (Bloomberg). The Volgograd industrial zone was struck on November 13 (Reuters). The Samara oil-pumping station was hit on November 14 (Bloomberg). Expect at least two to four more significant strikes on Russian fuel and logistics infrastructure before November 21. Russia will respond with missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian power plants, railways, and food factories. The winter blackout risk in Ukraine will worsen as temperatures drop. Confidence: almost certain more strikes on both sides; probable that at least one major Russian refinery or port is hit again.

RUSSIAN DOMESTIC SECURITY AND CAR BOMBINGS. Possible: the two car bombings in Moscow within 48 hours (November 12 and 13) suggest a targeted campaign, possibly by Ukrainian intelligence or pro-Ukrainian factions. Expect heightened security in Moscow and St Petersburg. There may be one or two more targeted incidents, but a full wave of bombings is less likely in a single week. The Kaliningrad treason trial and the arrest of Polish spies suggest Russia is tightening its internal security net. Confidence: possible one more targeted incident; unlikely a major wave of domestic violence.

OIL AND DIESEL MARKET. Probable: the Russian diesel situation will remain messy. The US tanker U-turn (WSJ, Bloomberg) means the deal is not dead but not working. Russia will court Brazilian and other buyers (Reuters). Crude prices will be influenced by the Shenzhen summit outcome. If Trump and Putin signal a broader deal, oil may dip; if the summit is muted, prices hold. The IEA data showing a rebound in Russian exports (Reuters, CNBC) will be cited by both sides. Confidence: probable continued volatility; possible a small dip in crude prices after the summit.

SPORTS DISPUTES. Probable: the IIHF CAS challenge (Reuters) will be briefed or heard. Russia's threats of sanctions against Canada and Germany (DW) will generate more headlines. The World Juniors and figure skating worlds will remain in flux. No resolution expected this week. Confidence: probable the dispute continues; unlikely a final ruling before November 21.

NUCLEAR ARMS DISCUSSION. Probable: the Shenzhen summit will produce some language on a new or revised nuclear arms framework, but the actual negotiations will be technical and slow. Trump's goal is to get a headline; Putin's goal is to reset the strategic balance in Russia's favor. Xi will try to position China as a neutral broker. Expect a joint communique that sounds important but is vague on specifics. Confidence: probable a statement on nuclear arms; possible a framework for technical talks; unlikely a signed treaty.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES (things that could happen but I would not bet heavily on):
- A sudden Russian offer to include the EU in the next round of talks, reversing Putin's earlier "pick one envoy" stance, if the Shenzhen summit goes well for him. (Possible, not probable.)
- A third car bombing or a more dramatic assassination in Moscow, escalating the domestic tension. (Possible.)
- A Russian cyberattack on European infrastructure in response to the new EU sanctions package, going beyond the Romanian incident. (Possible.)
- The US soldier espionage case in the UK being formally charged and generating a diplomatic spat. (Probable the charge is filed; the spasm is possible.)
- Russia announcing a new mobilization wave or a significant shift in front-line strategy, timed to the summit. (Unlikely to probable; Russia is more likely to use the summit as a stalling tool than to escalate.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON:
- A full ceasefire or armistice signed this week. The talks are moving, but the gap between Russia's demands and Ukraine's positions is still wide. (Unlikely.)
- A major Russian offensive on the ground, like a new push toward a major city. Russia is in a defensive-stall posture while diplomacy is in play. (Unlikely.)
- The ruble crashing or a full-blown capital flight crisis triggered by the EU sanctions. The package is incremental, not transformative. (Unlikely.)
- Putin stepping down, being seen in a hospital, or any succession drama. He is meeting Trump and Xi in five days; he will not make a move now. (Very unlikely.)
- A Russian nuclear test or a dramatic escalation of the satellite race. The satellite networks are being built, but no launch event is expected. (Unlikely.)

delta.motion:
Between the two photographs, five days apart, the diplomatic engine accelerated dramatically while the military escalation on Russian soil intensified in ways that were not fully visible in the first picture. The Abu Dhabi talks went from 'expected to begin around November 10' to actually happening on the 10th and 11th, producing the largest prisoner exchange of the war, and then the US sent Witkoff and Kushner straight to Moscow on the 12th. That is a three-step diplomatic jump in five days, and it was not in the first photograph at all. The Trump-Xi-Putin summit went from 'being actively planned' to formally announced for November 19 in Shenzhen, with the White House confirming Trump will raise nuclear-arms cuts. That is a new, hard, dated event that did not exist in the first picture.

The military theme grew in both intensity and geographic reach. The first photograph showed Russia striking Ukraine's energy grid and Ukraine hitting Russian refineries. The second photograph shows 1,200 drones launched at Russia in a single day, the ninth refinery of November hit including the biggest one in Siberia, a warship struck in the Gulf of Finland, a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, and two car bombs in Moscow within two days. The war came home to Russia in a more visceral, urban, almost domestic way than the first picture suggested. The casualty numbers also crept up: from 'around 400,000' to 'over 400,000' and one outlet reporting 450,000, with over 11,000 foreign military deaths now recorded.

The fuel and energy crisis persisted and deepened in the same way. Petrol rationing continued, the diesel deal stumbled further as a tanker made a U-turn off the US East Coast, and US companies kept shunning Russian fuel. But there is a new wrinkle: Russian oil revenues hit a five-month high and diesel exports to other markets doubled, suggesting the crisis is uneven and that Russia is redirecting rather than simply losing. The yuan-replacement push collapsed, which is a new thread not present in the first picture.

The Japan Tobacco seizure, which was a headline in the first photograph, shrank to background noise by the second. It is still generating friction but is no longer the dominant corporate story. In its place, a new sanctions theme grew: the EU agreed new listings on Russian banks, the shadow fleet, and misinformation operations, with a formal package due Monday November 17. The UK sanctioned Slavneft. Putin ordered a sanctioned bank to seize a UK brokerage's assets. Sanctions moved from a background condition to an active, escalating front.

The media and press-freedom theme held steady and grew slightly in symbolic weight. Novaya Gazeta's closure was confirmed and amplified, two French deputies and two journalists were barred from entering Russia, and Sberbank doubled down on AI after a drone hit its data center. The information-war thread is persistent but not dramatically different.

The ice hockey dispute shrank from a major story to a mid-tier one. The IIHF filed a CAS challenge, Russia threatened sanctions on Canada and Germany, and more countries joined the boycott, but the story no longer dominates the way it did in the first picture. It is now a sideshow with occasional flare-ups.

The Starlink-rival and space theme shrank slightly. It is still mentioned as Russia and Ukraine racing to build military satellite networks, but it is no longer a standalone headline. It has been absorbed into the broader technology and communications story.

A new theme appeared that was not in the first photograph: espionage and intelligence activity. A US Army soldier in a NATO unit was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia. Russia arrested two suspected Polish spies in Kaliningrad. Romania identified a Russian-linked cyber attack. Norway warned of possible sabotage in the coming year. The UK and Russia discussed a new back channel. This is a cluster of events that was not present in the first picture and represents a new layer of shadow confrontation.

Domestic politics also produced new items: a lawyer in Kaliningrad sentenced to 12 years for treason, police raiding Moscow gathering spots for young people, the ambassador to the US dying suddenly at 66, a visit to Afghanistan to discuss trade with the Taliban, and the bear-cull limits after 36 attacks. These are small but they fill out a domestic picture that was thinner in the first photograph.

The overall speed of motion is fast. The diplomatic track moved from planning to execution to follow-up in five days. The military track escalated from 'massive strikes' to 1,200 drones in a day and car bombs in the capital. The sanctions track moved from anticipation to agreement to a dated formal package. The APEC summit went from rumor to confirmed date and city. Russia is being compressed on multiple timelines simultaneously.
delta.wind:
The expectation that Abu Dhabi talks would happen was almost certain, and they did, on November 10 and 11. The expectation was that they would produce 'a framework document or a statement of intent' with both sides claiming partial success. What actually happened was slightly better for the process: the largest prisoner exchange of the war, which is a concrete, human result that goes beyond a framework document. Russia's negotiator Medinsky reported 'some progress' but no breakthrough, which matches the 'no full deal' prediction. The expectation that Russia would enter with a tough posture was confirmed: Putin was described as 'uncompromising' and 'playing for time.' The expectation that Melania Trump would continue her intermediary role was partially wrong; her presence in the second photograph is much less prominent, and the direct US envoys (Witkoff, Kushner) became the main channel instead. The expectation that the APEC summit would bring 'logistics announcements and diplomatic positioning' was understated: the summit was formally announced with a specific date (November 19) and location (Shenzhen), which is a bigger step than 'logistics announcements.' The expectation that a full peace deal was unlikely was correct; no deal was signed.

The expectation of continued strikes was almost certain, and it was exceeded. The prediction was 'at least one more significant strike on each side' and 'at least one high-casualty event on each side.' What happened was 1,200 drones in a single day, the ninth refinery hit, a warship struck, a port fire, and two car bombs in Moscow. The scale of the drone assault and the urban car bombs went beyond the 'at least one significant strike' framing. The double-tap targeting of emergency services was not specifically mentioned in the second photograph, so that pattern may have paused or simply not been reported. The expectation that Russia's dwindling land gains and record losses would make it harder to claim momentum was confirmed: the 400,000-plus casualty figure is now a recurring headline, and the 46-square-miles-in-ten-months stat from the first photograph is now background context.

The fuel crisis expectation was probable, and it held. Petrol rationing continued, the diesel deal stumbled with the tanker U-turn, and US companies kept shunning the fuel. The expectation of 'more budget-related announcements' was partially met: the yuan push collapsing and foreign businesses funding the war are new economic threads. The expectation that the 1 percent GDP growth would be used by the Kremlin was not specifically tested this week, but the oil-revenue rebound gives Moscow a mixed narrative to work with.

The Japan Tobacco expectation was probable for 'continued diplomatic sparring,' and that held, but the story shrank in prominence. The expectation of 'possibly another corporate seizure' did not materialize as a new headline; instead, the seizure theme broadened into the sanctions context (Putin ordering a bank to seize a UK brokerage's assets). The expectation that the stock-market impact would settle was correct; the limit-down days are now history.

The media and information-war expectation was probable for 'at least one new cyber or information-war incident,' and that was met: the French journalists being barred, the Sberbank AI/data-center story, and the ongoing Novaya Gazeta aftermath. The deepfake and social-media manipulation threads continued but were not the dominant headline. The expectation that the Novaya Gazeta closure would be framed differently by state and independent media was correct.

The ice hockey expectation was probable for 'continued public sparring' and unlikely for resolution, and that held exactly. The IIHF filed a CAS challenge, Russia threatened sanctions on Canada and Germany, and more countries joined the boycott. The expectation that this would be 'low-stakes but high-noise' was accurate.

The winter heating expectation was possible, and it partially materialized: Kyiv is facing winter blackouts, and the fuel shortages in Russian regions make winter more uncomfortable. The expectation of 'more public complaints and possibly local protests' was not strongly confirmed; the Moscow police raids on youth gathering spots hint at social tension but are not yet a fuel-price protest.

The Starlink-rival expectation was possible for 'at least one announcement,' and that was partially met: Russia and Ukraine are still described as racing to build military satellite networks, but no specific launch or announcement dominated the headlines. The satellite-attack rehearsal was not confirmed as a major incident this week.

Things that were not expected but came: the US soldier arrested in the UK for spying for Russia is a new espionage thread that was not in the expectation list. The two car bombs in Moscow, one a targeted assassination near St Petersburg, are a more urban and personal form of the war than the 'at least one high-casualty event' framing suggested. The 'beer-loving nations alliance' (UK, Netherlands, Baltic states) against Russian naval activity is a new and somewhat lighthearted diplomatic formation. The collapse of Russia's yuan-replacement push is a specific economic development not in the expectations. The formal announcement of the APEC summit with a date and city was faster and more concrete than the 'logistics announcements' expectation. The EU sanctions package being dated to Monday November 17 is a new hard deadline.

Things that did not come: a full peace deal (as predicted, unlikely). A mass Moscow street protest over fuel or the war (as predicted, unlikely). The Novaya Gazeta closure being reversed (as predicted, very unlikely). A sudden Russian ceasefire timed to the talks (as predicted, possible but not probable). A new major Russian ground offensive (as predicted, unlikely). Putin making a surprise personal visit to the US or China (as predicted, unlikely; the APEC summit is still future). A second major corporate seizure beyond Japan Tobacco (as predicted, possible; did not appear as a new headline).

What this says about the way expectations have been wrong for Russia: the diplomatic acceleration was faster and more concrete than predicted. The expectation framework treated the talks as a process that would produce documents and statements. In reality, the talks produced a prisoner exchange (a human, tangible result), and the US immediately escalated to direct Moscow visits within the same week. The US is moving faster and more personally than the expectation model assumed. The military escalation on Russian soil was more dramatic and more urban than the 'at least one significant strike' framing captured. The expectation model treated the strikes as a back-and-forth between two countries' infrastructure. In reality, the war is entering Moscow's streets with car bombs and hitting its warships in the Gulf of Finland. The espionage theme was entirely absent from the expectations and appeared as a cluster of arrests and warnings. The expectation model was weighted toward the war and the diplomacy and underweighted the shadow intelligence competition. The sanctions theme was also underweighted; it moved from background to an active, dated, escalating front in five days. Overall, the expectation model was directionally correct on the big themes but understated the speed of diplomatic escalation, the urban intensity of the military conflict, and the emergence of espionage and sanctions as active, front-page stories.
delta.driver: The force pushing Russia from the first photograph to the second is the collision between the US's aggressive, personal, time-compressed diplomatic push and Russia's simultaneous need to project strength while its fuel tanks run low and its casualty numbers climb past 400,000. Trump is not just mediating; he is flying envoys to Moscow within days of the Abu Dhabi sessions, locking in a three-way summit with Xi for November 19, and positioning the US as the indispensable broker. This compresses Russia's decision-making timeline and forces it to choose between holding a hard line (which it is doing, calling itself 'uncompromising') and accepting that every week of stalling costs it fuel, refinery capacity, and diplomatic goodwill. The underlying physical constraint is winter: the refineries are damaged, the petrol is being rationed, the diesel deal is stumbling, and the heating season is arriving. Russia cannot afford to let the war drag on without a diplomatic exit that preserves its core territorial claims, but it also cannot concede visibly while its own cities are hit with car bombs and its warships are struck in the Gulf of Finland. The APEC summit in Shenzhen is the hard deadline that will force a position, and the US is using it as leverage to extract concessions on nuclear arms and the Ukraine framework. In short, time, fuel, and the personal involvement of three heads of state are squeezing Russia into a narrower window of acceptable outcomes than it had five days ago, and the strikes on Russian soil are both a bargaining chip and a symptom of the urgency.

The format dispute between the US and China (Washington balked at Beijing's demand for a tightly scripted agenda) will either be resolved behind the scenes or will show in the body language of the photo op. The Yalta-1945 comparison will be in every headline. I expect a joint statement or a coordinated set of individual statements referencing nuclear arms, the Ukraine framework, and possibly a new European security architecture, but not a signed peace deal. Russia will enter with a hard line, as Putin was 'uncompromising' to Witkoff and Kushner in Moscow on November 12. The prisoner exchange from Abu Dhabi will be cited as proof of momentum. Zelensky will call it a 'window of opportunity' and push for European participation. The EU's unresolved question of who to send as a single envoy will create friction at the margins. China will position itself as a neutral broker while protecting its own trade interests. The summit will produce a photo, a statement, and a week of interpretation, but not a breakthrough. Confidence: very high that the summit happens as scheduled; high that it produces some form of joint or coordinated statement; medium that the nuclear-arms discussion produces a concrete next step; low that a full Ukraine framework is agreed.

EU SANCTIONS PACKAGE AND RUSSIAN COUNTERMEASURES (NOVEMBER 17). The EU's new sanctions listings on Russian banks, the shadow fleet, and misinformation operations are formally due for approval on Monday, November 17. This is a hard, dated event that will generate headlines across European and Russian media. The UK's sanctioning of Slavneft and Putin's order for a sanctioned bank to seize a UK brokerage's assets establish the pattern: Russia responds to each sanctions package with a targeted counter-move. I expect Russia to announce at least one concrete countermeasure within 48 hours of the EU vote: a new asset seizure, a targeted ban on a European company or bank, or a retaliatory trade restriction. The shadow-fleet listings will generate operational headaches for Russian oil exports, but the five-month-high oil revenues and the doubling of diesel exports to non-US markets suggest Russia has already begun redirecting. The sanctions will be framed in Moscow as 'coordinated European pressure' and in Brussels as 'a necessary step toward a credible framework.' Confidence: very high that the EU package is approved on or around November 17; high that Russia announces a countermeasure within a few days; medium that the countermeasure targets a specific, named European entity.

MILITARY ESCALATION ON RUSSIAN SOIL AND IN UKRAINE. The pattern of the past week is clear: 1,200 drones in a single day, the ninth refinery of November hit (including the biggest in Siberia), a warship struck in the Gulf of Finland, a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, and two car bombs in Moscow within two days. Ukraine is shifting toward urban, high-visibility targets inside Russia, not just industrial infrastructure. I expect at least two or three more significant strikes on Russian soil in the coming week, with a meaningful probability of another urban incident (a car bomb, a targeted assassination, or a drone strike on a building in a major city). Russia will continue striking Ukrainian energy, transport, and food infrastructure, worsening winter blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. The casualty numbers will continue to climb: the 400,000-plus Russian killed figure and the 11,000-plus foreign military deaths will be cited in new reports. The 46-square-miles-in-ten-months stat will remain background context, reinforcing the narrative of a grinding, costly war. Russia will not launch a major new ground offensive, but it will maintain pressure on the eastern and southern fronts. The satellite and military-communications race will continue as a background thread. Confidence: very high that significant strikes occur on both sides; high that at least one strike hits a Russian urban or port target; medium that a high-casualty event (20+ killed) occurs in a single incident; low that a new major ground offensive is launched.

FUEL, ENERGY, AND WINTER. Winter is arriving and the fuel crisis is deepening. Petrol rationing in several Russian regions will continue and may expand as refinery damage accumulates. The diesel deal with the US will see another stumble or a partial, grudging resolution: the tanker U-turn off the US East Coast and the shunning of Russian fuel by US companies suggest the deal is not yet working, but the political pressure from Trump (who will be in Shenzhen on November 19) may force a compromise. Russian oil revenues at a five-month high and the doubling of diesel exports to other markets give Moscow some breathing room, but the yuan-replacement collapse means Russia is still dependent on a fragmented, sanctions-affected trading system. Kyiv will face worsening winter blackouts as Russia strikes power infrastructure. Public complaints in Russian regions about fuel prices and availability will grow, though a mass street protest remains unlikely. The Sberbank AI and data-center story (after a drone hit) will generate further coverage as Russia pushes to modernize its military communications. Confidence: high that fuel rationing continues or expands; high that the diesel deal sees another complication; medium that a partial resolution is announced around the APEC summit; low that a mass fuel-price protest occurs in Moscow.

ESPIONAGE AND INTELLIGENCE. The cluster of espionage events this week (US Army soldier arrested in the UK for suspected Russian spying, two Polish spies arrested in Kaliningrad, a Russian-linked cyber attack identified in Romania, Norway's warning of possible sabotage, the UK-Russia back-channel discussion) is a new and persistent theme that the prior expectation model missed. I expect the US soldier case to generate diplomatic friction between London and Moscow, possibly a formal note or a low-level exchange. The UK-Russia back-channel will continue, and the Norway warning of possible sabotage in the coming year will be cited in European security briefings. There is a reasonable probability of one more arrest or revelation in Europe involving a Russian-linked operative or cyber incident. The Sberbank data-center drone hit and the broader military-satellite race will keep the intelligence-technology thread alive. Confidence: medium-high that the US soldier case generates a diplomatic response; medium that one more espionage-related arrest or revelation occurs in Europe; low that a major cyberattack on a single European financial institution occurs.

MEDIA, PRESS FREEDOM, AND INFORMATION WAR. Novaya Gazeta's closure of its Moscow newsroom will continue to generate commentary, both inside Russia and internationally. The barring of two French deputies and two journalists from entering Russia will be cited as evidence of a tightening information front. I expect at least one more media or information-war incident: a new cyberattack, a deepfake, a social-media manipulation story, or a further restriction on journalists. The state media will frame the Novaya Gazeta closure as 'a natural evolution' while independent and foreign media frame it as 'the last independent voice silenced.' The Russia-Ukraine information war will continue with both sides deploying battlefield narratives, possibly including new deepfake videos or hacked alert-app incidents. Confidence: high that Novaya Gazeta generates continued commentary; medium that one new information-war incident occurs; low that a major state-media reform or reversal is announced.

EUROPE'S ROLE AND THE ENVOY QUESTION. The EU's internal squabble over who to send as a single envoy to the Ukraine talks will remain unresolved, creating friction at the margins of the APEC summit. Zelensky will welcome European participation, and Putin will maintain that Europe can join if it shows 'readiness to contribute.' Germany's Merz will press Trump for 'no surprises' from the Putin talks. The EU's Ukraine funding measures due by year-end will be discussed but not finalized. The 'beer-loving nations alliance' (UK, Netherlands, Baltic states) against Russian naval activity will generate a small but persistent diplomatic thread. Confidence: medium that the envoy question is resolved before the end of the week; medium that the EU and Russia exchange pointed statements about European participation; low that a new European security framework is formally agreed.

ICE HOCKEY AND SPORTS. The dispute will continue as low-stakes, high-noise sparring. The IIHF's CAS challenge will be in the news, Russia will threaten or impose minor sanctions on Canada and Germany, and more European countries may join the boycott of Russian athletes. The NHL's position on Finland's block will be discussed. This is a sideshow, not a driver, but it generates consistent, low-intensity headlines. Confidence: high that the dispute continues without resolution; low that a compromise or CAS ruling changes the situation.

DOMESTIC POLITICS AND SOCIETY. The Kaliningrad lawyer's 12-year treason sentence and the police raids on Moscow youth gathering spots signal a tightening domestic grip. The sudden death of Russia's ambassador to the US at 66 will generate a brief news cycle and possibly a replacement announcement. The visit to Afghanistan to discuss trade with the Taliban will be a small but notable diplomatic thread. The bear-cull limits after 36 attacks are a small human-interest story. I do not expect a major domestic political event, but the social tension (youth raids, fuel rationing, casualty numbers) is building. Confidence: medium that the ambassador's death generates a replacement announcement; low that a significant domestic political crisis or protest occurs.

WHAT I WOULD NOT BET ON: A full peace deal signed in Shenzhen. A sudden Russian ceasefire timed to the summit. A major new Russian ground offensive. A mass Moscow street protest over fuel or the war. The Novaya Gazeta closure being reversed. A second major corporate seizure beyond the sanctions context. A nuclear test or exercise. A Black Sea attack on a non-belligerent vessel. Putin making a surprise personal concession on Donbas territory. The ice hockey dispute resolving before the end of the week.
crystal.headline: Putin, Trump, Xi Meet in Shenzhen as Drones and Sanctions Close In
emoji_reasons: The Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen on November 19 is the single most consequential event of the week, the first three-way meeting of the great powers.
The military escalation on Russian soil, with 1,200 drones in a day, car bombs in Moscow, and a warship struck, defines the war's new urban intensity.
The EU sanctions package due Monday November 17 and the expected Russian countermeasures mark the sanctions front as an active, dated, escalating thread.
crystal.tldr: The Trump-Xi-Putin summit in Shenzhen on November 19 will dominate the second half of the week, producing a joint statement on nuclear arms and the Ukraine framework but not a full peace deal. The EU's new sanctions package will be formally approved on November 17, triggering a Russian countermeasure. Military strikes on Russian soil will continue to escalate in both intensity and urban visibility, with a meaningful probability of another car bomb or targeted assassination in a major city.
crystal.eli5:
This week, three of the world's biggest leaders — the US president, the Chinese president, and the Russian president — are all flying to the same city in China to sit in a room together. It's the first time all three have met face-to-face, and everyone is watching to see if they can agree on anything, especially about nuclear weapons and the war in Ukraine. Think of it like three kids who've been arguing in the schoolyard finally being put in the same classroom by the principal. They'll probably shake hands and take a photo, but they won't necessarily agree on everything.

At the same time, the war is getting more intense and more personal for people living in Russia. Ukraine is sending huge waves of drones — over a thousand in a single day — and hitting oil refineries, a warship, and even dropping car bombs in Moscow. It's like the war, which used to feel like it was happening 'over there,' is now showing up in the streets of Russian cities. Meanwhile, Russia keeps hitting Ukraine's power plants and factories, making winter harder for people in Kyiv and other cities.

Europe is also stepping up. The EU is voting on a new set of rules that make it harder for Russia to do business and move its oil around the world. Russia will probably respond by grabbing some European company's assets, which is its usual move. And there's a whole undercurrent of spy stuff: a US soldier got arrested in the UK for allegedly spying for Russia, and there are arrests in Poland and Romania too. It's like the two sides are still playing a quiet game of cat-and-mouse even while they're trying to talk peace.

The fuel situation in Russia is getting worse as winter arrives. Gas stations are rationing, the deal to sell Russian diesel to the US keeps stumbling, and people in Russian regions are complaining about prices. But Russian oil revenues are actually at a five-month high because they're selling to other countries, so the picture is mixed: painful in some places, surprising in others.

The big question for the rest of the week is: does the Shenzhen meeting produce something real, or just a photo and a statement that both sides can spin as a win? Based on what's happened so far — the prisoner exchange, the 'uncompromising' Putin, the US pushing hard but not forcing a deal — the most likely outcome is a step forward, not a leap. The war doesn't end next week, but the diplomacy gets more personal and more public, and the strikes get more urban and more painful for ordinary Russians.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A captured the week's major themes with considerable accuracy. The Abu Dhabi talks prediction was spot-on: tense, no breakthrough, framework-level discussion, Russia demanding security-guarantee language, Ukraine pushing territorial concessions, Europe trying to insert itself, and the Kremlin complaining about European disunity. The 'three to five major headlines' estimate was conservative given the volume of coverage. The continued-strikes section was well-calibrated: a major Russian strike with significant casualties (14 killed at a train station, strikes on military factories, railways, food factories) and significant Ukrainian strikes inside Russia (9th refinery, 1,200-drone barrage, warship hit, Ust-Luga port fire, two car bombs in Moscow) all materialized. The 'double-tap' pattern observation and the 400,000-killed narrative were confirmed (the figure actually rose to 450,000). The fuel crisis prediction was accurate: petrol rationing was confirmed, the diesel deal stumbled with the tanker U-turn, and the 1% GDP figure remained in circulation. The Japan Tobacco / corporate seizure thread was confirmed by the Bloomberg piece on seized businesses funding the war and the UK brokerage asset seizure. The information-war section hit on Novaya Gazeta's closure, the French social-media manipulation, and a new cyber incident (Romanian-linked, Sberbank data-center drone attack). The ice-hockey section was correct: the CAS challenge, Canada and Finland blocking entry, Russia threatening sanctions, and the NHL note all appeared. The space section was confirmed by the satellite-network race and Starshield disruptions. The APEC summit was mentioned but somewhat understated as 'discussed as a future event, generating at least one headline about preparations or speculation'; in reality it became the week's single biggest forward-looking story, formally announced for November 19 in Shenzhen. The Europe section was over-specific: predictions about Bulgaria's Yotova, Serbia's bank closure, Moldova's power line, and Finland's tank barriers did not produce headlines this week, while the EU sanctions package (Nov 17) and the UK's Slavneft sanction were the actual European actions. The Russia-Iran section was less relevant this week than anticipated. A missed the espionage thread (US Army soldier arrested in the UK), the car-bomb tactic in Moscow, the ambassador's sudden death, the 'beer-loving nations alliance,' and the collapse of the yuan-replacement push. The 'less likely surprise' of a one-city ceasefire did not materialize, but the prisoner exchange (the largest of the war) was the concrete result, which A's 'framework document or joint statement' language roughly captured without naming it. Overall, A's picture of the week was substantially correct in direction and theme, with the main weakness being over-specificity on European sub-plot lines and slight underweighting of the APEC summit's prominence.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B also captured the week's major themes accurately and with slightly better calibration. The Abu Dhabi talks prediction was correct: talks happened, Russia was tough, no breakthrough, a framework-level outcome (the prisoner exchange as the concrete result), and both sides claiming partial success. The 'almost certain' confidence for the talks and strikes was well-placed. The APEC summit was explicitly flagged as 'probable as an announcement' in the less-likely-surprises section, and it did in fact get formally scheduled for November 19 in Shenzhen, becoming the week's dominant forward-looking story. This is a meaningful edge over A, which treated the summit more as background speculation. The continued-strikes section was accurate and appropriately measured: at least one significant strike on each side, double-tap patterns, and Russia's record losses all confirmed. The fuel crisis prediction was correct: rationing persisted, the diesel deal stumbled, and budget strain became visible. The Japan Tobacco section was right on continued diplomatic friction and the precedent rattling investors, and the Bloomberg piece on seized businesses funding the war confirmed the broader theme. The information-war section hit on Novaya Gazeta, the cyber incidents, and the hacked-apps thread. The ice-hockey section was accurate in its 'low-stakes but high-noise' characterization and the continued public sparring. The winter-heating section was a good addition that A lacked as a standalone theme, and it was confirmed: Kyiv faced winter blackouts, water shortages, and Ukraine's power supply was described as 'close to critical.' The space section was confirmed by the satellite-network race and Starshield restrictions. The 'things I would not bet on' list was mostly accurate: no full peace deal, no mass Moscow protest, no Novaya Gazeta reversal, no major ground offensive, no surprise Putin visit. B missed the espionage thread (US soldier arrested in UK), the car-bomb tactic, the ambassador's death, the 'beer-loving nations alliance,' and the yuan-replacement collapse, similar to A. The prisoner exchange as the concrete talks outcome was not specifically named, but B's 'framework document or statement of intent' language was close. The EU sanctions package (Nov 17) and the UK's Slavneft sanction were not specifically predicted but fit within B's general sanctions-and-economic-pressure framing. Overall, B's picture of the week was substantially correct, with the advantages of better confidence calibration, the explicit APEC-summit call, the winter-heating addition, and a useful negative list that helped a reader understand what was NOT coming.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts are strong and cover the same core themes: Abu Dhabi talks, continued mutual strikes, fuel crisis, corporate seizures, information war, ice hockey, space, and the APEC summit. Both correctly identified the diplomatic push as the week's dominant story, the strikes as a continuous escalation, the fuel crisis as a persistent domestic strain, Novaya Gazeta's closure as a symbolic blow, and the ice-hockey dispute as a low-stakes noise generator. Both missed the espionage thread, the car-bomb tactic in Moscow, the ambassador's death, and the 'beer-loving nations alliance.' The key differentiators are: (1) The APEC summit. B explicitly called it 'probable as an announcement' and framed it as logistics and diplomatic positioning, which is exactly what happened. A mentioned it but as background speculation. The summit became the week's single biggest forward-looking headline cluster. (2) Winter heating. B had a dedicated section on civilian winter impact, which was confirmed by Kyiv's blackouts, water shortages, and the 'close to critical' power supply. A mentioned infrastructure strikes but did not isolate the winter angle. (3) Calibration. B's confidence language ('almost certain,' 'probable,' 'possible') tracked the actual outcomes more cleanly. A's 'highly confident' on several items was fine, but the over-specific European sub-plot predictions (Bulgaria, Serbia, Moldova, Finland tank barriers) mostly did not materialize, while the actual European actions (EU sanctions package, UK Slavneft sanction) were less specifically predicted. (4) The 'things I would not bet on' list in B gave a reader a useful negative map that was largely accurate. (5) A's greater detail in the fuel-crisis and strikes sections was valuable and accurate, and the 'double-tap' observation was sharp. On balance, B's slightly better calibration, the explicit APEC-summit call, the winter-heating addition, and the useful negative list give it a narrow edge. A's over-specificity on European sub-plots that did not materialize and its underweighting of the APEC summit cost it a few points. Neither forecast was wrong on the big picture; both would have served a reader well. But B's more disciplined confidence language and the APEC call make it the slightly more useful document to have in hand on Monday morning. VERDICT: B
